addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# Todo

This file contains near term tasks with a short description
and reference links to more details.

Intro paragraphs in `## Todo` and `## Bugs` should begin every
line with 1 leading space so they don't match the `^\d+\. `
pattern that locates numbered entries; 2 or 3 spaces also work.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text **moves** here
(never copied; one home per text). The picked-up task is a
`###` heading; a multi-cycle program adds one level, where the
program is the `###` and its current stage a `####` (headings
give the current work durable anchors, which numbered Todo
entries can't). The problem overview is followed by the
"plan", a bulleted list of the development "ladder". Each
rung is prepended with its commit reference, a literal
`[[N]]` placeholder until the commit is pushed, then
backfilled to a real file-local `[[n]]` ref (same pattern as
the chores As-built rungs):
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

### Refactor: typed jj facade -> jj-lib in-process; end subprocess spawning

Version-control operations were ~30 hand-rolled `run("jj", ...)`
spawns plus every mutation, with per-module private wrappers
and raw-git vestiges in init: stderr parsing instead of typed
errors, and jj's single-attempt index-lock acquisition (the
push `bookmark-set` lock race in [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md))
can't be retried where it fails. A multi-ladder program; the
staged plan, design detail, and the eight absorbed former
Todos live in
[refactor-20260716.md](notes/refactor-20260716.md).

Program ladder in **straight trunk order**, one bullet per
commit that lands on the branch, so reading it top to bottom
is reading `git log --first-parent`. `refactor:` entries are
the program's rungs, one per cycle (adjacent stages
consolidated 2026-07-24; titles are the anticipated close-out
titles; unshipped versions are provisional, since jj-lib may
split into two cycles). `docs:` entries are interludes that
sit between cycles and belong to no rung. Every shipped ref
points at a close-out commit on `refactor-vc-x1`, treated as
permanent: the branch is long-lived and lands on main
merge-only, never rebased.

The order is load-bearing: a
trapezoid's `<base>` is the parent of its own first rung, not
the previous close-out, so 0.78.0 bases on 0.77.4. Taking the
close-out instead swallows the interludes into the merge's
ladder side, which already bit at 0.76.0, whose base was the
0.75.1 interlude. See
[the recipe](notes/cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe).

2	
3	Checklists for the moments where slips happen: committing, pushing, closing out. The full
4	protocol, with rationale and recovery procedures, is

6	the relevant checklist immediately before the action; don't run it from memory.

9	[custom.md](../custom.md).

11	## The cycle at a glance
12	
13	Every change runs as a **cycle**: Preparation (`X.Y.Z-0`, optional) -> Work commits
14	(`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...) -> Close-out (bare `X.Y.Z`). The version suffix encodes the phase;
15	the scheme, and where the version-of-record lives, are in
16	[versioning.md](../notes/versioning.md). Read [cycle-protocol.md](../notes/cycle-protocol.md)
17	before any commit work, and before any push, cycle or not.
18	
19	## Committing vs pushing
20	
21	A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`; never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
22	commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
23	`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)); a
24	pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate (bugs.md #6). In
25	an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
26	is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
27	publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
28	around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
29	cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#policy).
30	
31	## Per-commit checklist
32	
33	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
34	[Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):
35	
36	1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
37	2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
38	3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit.
39	4. Validate the artifact (the medium-specific commands are in [custom.md](../custom.md)).
40	   Skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out.
41	5. Say "ready to commit" and stop. The user reviews the working-copy diff; iterate until
42	   complete.
43	6. Write the description: <=72-col conventional title, prose body (work repo: file-by-file,
44	   opening with the version-bump bullet). See
45	   [Commit description](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
46	7. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
47	   explicitly includes it.
48	8. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
49	   `jj commit`; never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.
50	
51	## Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist
52	
53	Within a sub-cycle ladder, per the protocol's
54	[per-Work-commit contract](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder):
55	
56	1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@`.
57	2. Do the commit's work.
58	3. Run the fast validation (named in [custom.md](../custom.md)). Non-negotiable.
59	4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: scratch working title. This first-time authoring is
60	   the one permitted describe; the commit is never published and never carries a trailer.
61	
62	Nothing on a ladder is pushed; the close-out squash
63	(`jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`) collapses it, and `vc-x1 push` then
64	publishes the single commit.
65	
66	## Before any push
67	
68	- This specific push has the user's explicit approval. Approval of a plan that includes a push
69	  is not push approval; "commit and push" names the destination, not a waiver of the reviews.
70	  Only an explicit scoped delegation ("do all of X, don't check in") waives the stops, for that
71	  bounded task only; destructive ops still pause.
72	- Validation ran, and passed, after the last edit.
73	- Closing words are already written; nothing follows the turn's final push (next checklist).
74	
75	## After the final push: hard stop
76	
77	Once the turn's final push or bot-repo squash-push is invoked, do no further work: no
78	verification, no summary, no next-step offers, no edits, until the user speaks. Put all closing
79	words *before* the invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a visible token
80	after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary
81	or more work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's direction. A standing
82	delegation makes intermediate pushes just steps; the hard stop lands on the turn's *final*
83	push. See
84	[After push or squash-push](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).
85

87

89	[Close-out](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#close-out):
90	
91	1. Move the picked-up item from `## In Progress` to a one-line `## Done` entry with its chores
92	   `[N]` ref.
93	2. Finalize the chores section: sync the header to the final commit title (and every anchor
94	   back-reference), add design subsections; the intro and As-built rungs are already there.
95	3. Full validation, mandatory.
96	4. Update `notes/README.md` if functionality changed.
97	5. At push time, surface the shape options (squash / trapezoid / keep separate) and wait for
98	   the user's choice. The trapezoid recipe is
99	   [in the protocol](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe); its step 4 is
100	   `jj git push`, not `vc-x1 push`.
101	6. Backfill `Commits:` / ladder refs for the commits the previous push made permanent; never
102	   record a SHA that is not on a permanent branch.
103	
104	## vc-x1 push behaviors to keep in mind
105	
106	Three, independent of project language:
107	
108	- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 assumes nothing about a repo's contents beyond
109	  `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`, and runs no build or tests. The medium's validation is the
110	  per-commit flow's job, run *before* invoking `vc-x1 push`. The one check that remains is
111	  `push-work` verifying the bookmark's remote refs are tracked, which is its own precondition.
112	- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume. Every stage no-ops when its
113	  work is already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If a run fails, push stops and
114	  reports; getting the repos back to a sensible state is the user's call, not something the
115	  tool infers.
116	- **ochid trailers** are injected by `vc-x1 push` itself, so don't hand-write them into the
117	  commit body or `--title`/`--body`.

1	# Code conventions
2	
3	Conventions for source code. Read this before writing code. The Rust-specific sections apply
4	wherever the medium is a Rust crate (see [custom.md](../custom.md) for the project's medium).
5	
6	Universal file, pinned to vc-x1-work-repo-template; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
7	[custom.md](../custom.md).
8	
9	## Line width
10	
11	Source lines, including doc comments and inline comments, wrap at <=100 cols (rustfmt's
12	default `max_width`; the per-commit flow's `cargo fmt` enforces it for code, and the same limit
13	applies to the comment text it doesn't reflow).
14	
15	## Doc comments on every file, function, and method
16	
17	Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every function and method must have
18	a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief: one sentence of purpose is often enough; the discipline
19	is that the comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
20	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).
21	
22	This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments" default that applies to
23	inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the module / item surface are expected; inline
24	explanatory comments inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
25	non-obvious WHY.
26	
27	**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive `--help` output. Clap reflows
28	by default and collapses bullets into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
29	any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on its own line in the rendered
30	help.
31	
32	## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)
33	
34	The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
35	`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
36	patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a
37	lean, not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
38	in scope:
39	
40	- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
41	- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a
42	  silently substituted value that can hide a wrong result.
43	
44	When one is used, three obligations attach:
45	
46	- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
47	  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
48	    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
49	  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
50	    `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")`, where an empty desc gives an empty title).
51	  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment). Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are
52	    not used because they require a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
53	- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so the site gets reviewed and
54	  appropriate uses are learned. Don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
55	- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the site, because Rust projects
56	  enable the project-wide lints in `Cargo.toml`:
57	
58	  ```toml
59	  [lints.clippy]
60	  unwrap_used = "warn"
61	  expect_used = "warn"
62	  ```
63	
64	  Every panicking site is then opt-in and visible in the diff; clippy (in the per-commit flow)
65	  catches any that slip through. The `_or*` siblings have no clippy lint; they are covered by

# Code conventions

Conventions for source code. Read this before writing code. The Rust-specific sections apply
wherever the medium is a Rust crate (see [custom.md](../custom.md) for the project's medium).

Universal file, pinned to vc-x1-work-repo-template; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
[custom.md](../custom.md).

## Line width

Source lines, including doc comments and inline comments, wrap at <=100 cols (rustfmt's
default `max_width`; the per-commit flow's `cargo fmt` enforces it for code, and the same limit
applies to the comment text it doesn't reflow).

## Doc comments on every file, function, and method

Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every function and method must have
a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief: one sentence of purpose is often enough; the discipline
is that the comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).

This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments" default that applies to
inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the module / item surface are expected; inline
explanatory comments inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
non-obvious WHY.

**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive `--help` output. Clap reflows
by default and collapses bullets into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on its own line in the rendered
help.

## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)

The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a
lean, not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
in scope:

- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a
  silently substituted value that can hide a wrong result.

When one is used, three obligations attach:

- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
    `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")`, where an empty desc gives an empty title).
  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment). Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are
    not used because they require a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so the site gets reviewed and
  appropriate uses are learned. Don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the site, because Rust projects
  enable the project-wide lints in `Cargo.toml`:

  ```toml
  [lints.clippy]
  unwrap_used = "warn"
  expect_used = "warn"
  ```

  Every panicking site is then opt-in and visible in the diff; clippy (in the per-commit flow)
  catches any that slip through. The `_or*` siblings have no clippy lint; they are covered by
  the comment convention and the conversational alert. (The vc-x1-work-repo-template's
  `CargoRust.toml` seeds a base `Cargo.toml` with this section already in place.)

```rust
let max = stderr_level.unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Info); // OK: default verbosity when -v/-vv absent
let first_line = desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("");  // OK: obvious

match matches.len() {
    1 => {
        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]
        // OK: `1 =>` arm guarantees matches.len() == 1
        Ok(TitleMatch::One(matches.into_iter().next().unwrap()))
    }
    // ...
}
```

Tests (`#[cfg(test)]`) are exempt, since panicking on setup failure is the correct test
behavior.

## Stage: jj-lib migration

Migrate the facade internals to jj-lib (already a dependency
for read-only commands); removes jj and git spawning
entirely.

- Reads first: `jj log` templates become `Commit` accessors
  (the `src/jj.rs` facade internals; `common::load_repo` /
  `resolve_revset` are the existing in-process machinery).
  Caveat: queries against `@` rely on the spawned CLI's
  working-copy auto-snapshot, since push asks "uncommitted
  changes *right now*?", so the in-process form must
  snapshot first, and a snapshot is an op-store write:
  those reads move with the mutation lift, not before.
- Then mutations: commit, describe, bookmark set/track,
  fetch, push, which is the workspace/transaction/op-store
  lift.
- The index-lock retry loop becomes ours (catch, back off,
  retry) with real error types, the fix vehicle for the
  bugs.md `bookmark-set` lock race [[1]].
- `LocalBareInit`'s `git init --bare` becomes a gix call
  (jj-lib already pulls gix in).

## Stage: push body-intro validation

Runs as the first rung of the
[trapezoid close-out](#stage-trapezoid-close-out) cycle
(2026-07-24 consolidation); its "after jj-lib" placement
was program order, not a dependency.

A bullet-first commit body trips jj's arg parser today
(`-m "<body>"` reads the leading `-` as a stray flag; hit on
0.62.0-5) and push fails with an opaque error.

- Validate the body opens with a non-dash intro line (Prose
  Form) and report the offending first line with a clear,
  specific error. Enforcing the intro is the intended
  behavior, not a parser fix.

1	//! Typed facade over `jj` subprocess queries.
2	//!
3	//! Every read-only `jj log -T <template>` / `jj bookmark list`
4	//! spawn goes through this module — primitives plus typed
5	//! helpers — so call sites stop hand-rolling argument lists (the
6	//! DRY-facade stage of `notes/refactor-20260716.md`):
7	//!
8	//! - `log` — the raw primitive; the helpers below cover the
9	//!   common templates.
10	//! - `matches` / `rev_exists` — does a revset match / does a
11	//!   revision resolve.
12	//! - `chid_of` / `cid_of` / `cid_short_of` — change / commit ids.
13	//! - `desc_of` / `is_empty` — description and emptiness.
14	//!
15	//! Mutations still spawn `jj` at their call sites; the jj-lib
16	//! migration stage moves both in-process.
17	
18	use std::path::Path;
19	
20	use crate::common::run;
21	
22	/// Crate-standard boxed-error result, aliased locally for brevity.
23	type Result<T> = std::result::Result<T, Box<dyn std::error::Error>>;
24	
25	/// Run `jj log -r <rev> --no-graph -T <template> -R <repo>` and
26	/// return its stdout (`run` trims surrounding whitespace).
27	pub fn log(repo: &Path, rev: &str, template: &str) -> Result<String> {
28	    run(
29	        "jj",
30	        &[
31	            "log",
32	            "-r",
33	            rev,
34	            "--no-graph",
35	            "-T",
36	            template,
37	            "-R",
38	            &repo.to_string_lossy(),
39	        ],
40	        Path::new("."),
41	    )
42	}
43	
44	/// True when `revset` matches at least one commit in `repo`.
45	///
46	/// A valid-but-empty revset (e.g. `conflicts()` on a clean repo)
47	/// is `Ok(false)`; an unresolvable revision is an `Err` — use
48	/// `rev_exists` to fold that case to `false`.
49	pub fn matches(repo: &Path, revset: &str) -> Result<bool> {
50	    Ok(!log(repo, revset, "\"x\"")?.is_empty())
51	}
52	
53	/// True when `rev` resolves in `repo`.
54	///
55	/// Maps jj's unresolvable-revision errors (`doesn't exist`,
56	/// `No such revision`) to `Ok(false)`; other failures (bad repo
57	/// path, spawn error) stay `Err`.
58	pub fn rev_exists(repo: &Path, rev: &str) -> Result<bool> {
59	    match matches(repo, rev) {
60	        Ok(found) => Ok(found),
61	        Err(e) => {
62	            let msg = e.to_string();
63	            if msg.contains("doesn't exist") || msg.contains("No such revision") {
64	                Ok(false)
65	            } else {
66	                Err(e)
67	            }
68	        }
69	    }
70	}
71	
72	/// The 12-character change id of `rev`.
73	pub fn chid_of(repo: &Path, rev: &str) -> Result<String> {
74	    log(repo, rev, "change_id.short(12)")
75	}
76	
77	/// The full commit id of `rev`.
78	pub fn cid_of(repo: &Path, rev: &str) -> Result<String> {
79	    log(repo, rev, "commit_id")
80	}
81	
82	/// The 12-character commit id of `rev`.
83	pub fn cid_short_of(repo: &Path, rev: &str) -> Result<String> {
84	    log(repo, rev, "commit_id.short(12)")
85	}
86	
87	/// The full description (title + body) of `rev`.
88	pub fn desc_of(repo: &Path, rev: &str) -> Result<String> {
89	    log(repo, rev, "description")
90	}
91	
92	/// True when `rev` is empty (no file changes relative to its
93	/// parent). Strict: anything but `true` / `false` from the
94	/// template is an error.
95	pub fn is_empty(repo: &Path, rev: &str) -> Result<bool> {
96	    let out = log(repo, rev, "empty")?;
97	    match out.as_str() {
98	        "true" => Ok(true),
99	        "false" => Ok(false),
100	        other => Err(format!("jj::is_empty: unexpected template output {other:?}").into()),
101	    }
102	}
103	
104	/// Run `jj bookmark list <bookmark> -R <repo>` and return its
105	/// stdout — empty when the local bookmark doesn't exist.
106	pub fn bookmark_list(repo: &Path, bookmark: &str) -> Result<String> {
107	    run(
108	        "jj",
109	        &["bookmark", "list", bookmark, "-R", &repo.to_string_lossy()],
110	        Path::new("."),
111	    )
112	}
113	
114	/// Like `bookmark_list` but with `-a`: includes remote refs —
115	/// tracked ones indented (`  @origin: …`), non-tracking at
116	/// column 0 (`<bookmark>@<remote>: …`). The input for
117	/// `common::find_tracked_remote` /
118	/// `common::find_non_tracking_remote`.
119	pub fn bookmark_list_all(repo: &Path, bookmark: &str) -> Result<String> {
120	    run(
121	        "jj",
122	        &[
123	            "bookmark",
124	            "list",
125	            "-a",
126	            bookmark,
127	            "-R",
128	            &repo.to_string_lossy(),
129	        ],
130	        Path::new("."),
131	    )
132	}
133

155	absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a record up with its commit.

173	chores section is the source of truth for the design thinking; the two cross-link, neither
174	restates the other.
175	
176	The section is **built up per commit**: each work commit appends its own `### As-built ladder`
177	rung + any narrative as it lands, rather than the narrative waiting for close-out (which only

189	places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; chores owns the

194	The first line under a chores section header is a `Commits:` line citing the git commit(s)
195	that section records:

197	```
198	## refactor: extract config loader
199	
200	Commits: [[3]]
201	
202	<intro paragraph...>
203	```
204	
205	`Commits:` uses the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
206	[Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render:
207	`Commits: [[3]]`, or `Commits: [[3]],[[5]]` for several. (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the
208	`[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]` resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and
209	CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The `# References` definition puts the **commit
210	URL** as the destination, with the **full 40-hex SHA** in the title slot:
211	
212	```
213	[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
214	```
215	
216	- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
217	  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
218	- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
219	  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
220	  say) gets the canonical identifier.
221	
222	**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
223	long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
224	can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every section opens with an
225	**empty `Commits:`**, and each push backfills the `Commits:` of the commits the previous push
226	made permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch lands. The commit itself is
227	the record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
228	[Commits backfill](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).

```

`Commits:` uses the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
[Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render:
`Commits: [[3]]`, or `Commits: [[3]],[[5]]` for several. (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the
`[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]` resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and
CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The `# References` definition puts the **commit
URL** as the destination, with the **full 40-hex SHA** in the title slot:

```
[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
```

- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
  say) gets the canonical identifier.

**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every section opens with an
**empty `Commits:`**, and each push backfills the `Commits:` of the commits the previous push
made permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch lands. The commit itself is
the record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
[Commits backfill](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).

##### 0.78.0-4 feat: jj-lib version gate

Implements [the policy](notes/jj-version-policy.md) written at
`-3`; the design questions were settled there and this rung
re-decides none of them.

Moved ahead of the reads rung when the ladder's own reason for
its position turned out to be wrong. "The gate lands before the
mutations, so mutations arrive in a repo that already refuses"
assumed the exposure arrives with the mutations. It did not:
`common::load_repo` has called `load_at_head` since the facade
moved to jj-lib, and it backs `chid`, `desc`, `list` and `show`.
Op-head merging and index reindexing have been happening
in-process, ungated, for several cycles. The hole is open now,
and `-5` would have widened it first.

The gate applies to every subcommand, with no list of exempt
ones. It first shipped in this rung's working copy with a
carve-out: an `opens_repo` method, an exhaustive `match` on
`Commands` with no wildcard arm, so a new subcommand would fail
to compile until someone picked a side. That was dropped at
review, unpushed, on an argument that holds:

- the match enforces enumeration, not classification. A new
  subcommand does force a decision; an existing one that grows a
  repo read later stays classified as safe, silently, and nothing
  fails.
- the policy called the carve-out "provably does not open a
  repo". The actual proof was a grep of five modules for
  `load_repo` and friends, which is a point-in-time observation
  wearing the word "provably".
- two of the costs claimed for keeping the list were not real.
  `--help` exits inside clap's `e.exit()` during parse, and
  completion exits inside `CompleteEnv::complete()` on main's
  first line, so neither ever reached the gate.

What remains is one rule with no list to maintain: every
subcommand except `version` refuses on a mismatch. The cost is
that a markdown linter needs a version-matched jj, which is what
the per-invocation override is for.

`jj -V` is spawned once per process and cached, not once per
operation. Ironic in the cycle that ends spawning, and
unavoidable: it is a spawn on their side of the boundary.

Three failures, not one, because the fix differs each time: `jj`
absent from `$PATH`, `jj -V` unreadable, and a genuine mismatch.
Only the third mentions `--allow-jj-mismatch`, since the override
is meaningless for the other two.

A measured over-strictness landed in the policy's known holes on
the way: `0.42` and `0.43` store the same bytes, so a vc-x1
linking `0.42` would refuse against `jj 0.43` while being safe to
run. The route to that finding is worth more than the finding.
The first evidence offered was that the `.proto` files are
identical, and the conclusion drawn from it, that the data cannot
have changed, was wrong: a fixed schema still permits the same
fields meaning different things, non-protobuf state like the
index segments moving, and content hashing changing so the same
data lands under different ids. Ruling those out took a source
diff across four files. Nobody will repeat that on every bump,
which argues *for* the blunt gate, and it demotes the schema
fingerprint from "makes an override provably safe" to "catches
one narrow class at build time".

The refusal path is what the test drives, with a fake `jj` first
on `PATH` reporting `0.99.0`: the real pair matches here, so a
test that only exercised the match would pin nothing. It checks
all four consequences at once, that a repo-opening command
refuses and names the override, that the override works, that a
markdown linter is unaffected, and that `version` still answers
while withholding the `jj-data` lines.

Measured 2026-07-31 against `jj 0.43.0`, both repos identical:
`commit=git op=simple_op_store op-heads=simple_op_heads_store
index=default submodule=default working-copy=local`.

491	destroy what the other wrote:
492	
493	- ours newer than theirs: we write fields their jj skips, and
494	  their next write drops them
495	- ours older than theirs: they wrote fields we skip, and our
496	  next write drops them
497	
498	Content addressing means the original blob survives under its
499	own id, so this is loss of current state rather than
500	destruction of history. The recorded rationale exempted the
501	second direction on the grounds that jj must support reading
502	its own older ops. That holds for jj reading. It stops holding
503	once our writes are in the picture, which they are. So the
504	test is `!=`, not an ordering comparison, and the reason is
505	better than the one we first wrote down.
506	
507	Equality is also the honest response to an unanswerable
508	question. We cannot compute compatibility, because the data
509	publishes no schema and jj publishes no stability policy. An
510	unequal pair is not "incompatible", it is "unknown", and the
511	only correct response to unknown on a path that writes is
512	stop.
513	
514	**Reads write, so the gate cannot be scoped to writes.**

521	  makes `DefaultIndexStore` reindex and write new segment

1	# Prose and durable text
2	
3	How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
4	commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
5	comments, chores sections).
6	
7	Universal file, pinned to vc-x1-work-repo-template; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
8	[custom.md](../custom.md).
9	
10	## Prose form
11	
12	Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why*
13	or the high-level *what*, then a `-` bullet list for the details. Wrap lines at <=100 cols,
14	commit titles and bodies at <=72 (bullet continuations indent two spaces); existing text
15	re-wraps when touched, no mass sweeps. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they hide the structure
16	that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their relationship is
17	the same failure at sentence scale; see [Semicolons inside bullets](#semicolons-inside-bullets)
18	and [Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
19	
20	Surfaces that use this shape:
21	
22	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files; see
23	  [Doc comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
24	- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The <=72-col title is the
25	  commit-specific add-on; see [Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
26	- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`; see
27	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
28	- Todo and Done entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure
29	  one-liners are still fine.
30	
31	Bullet *content* differs by surface:
32	
33	- **Commit bodies**: bullets are file-by-file, one bullet per file changed, file plus a
34	  one-line gist (e.g. `README.md: new Overview intro`), detail as sub-bullets in short sentence
35	  fragments (full sentences are discouraged). Source of truth for the mechanical edit list.
36	- **Chores / todo / done**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what
37	  landed and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit
38	  list; see
39	  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
40	- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).
41	
42	### Problem + plan shape
43	
44	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores section intros, and `## Todo` entries use a sharper form
45	of the same shape:
46	
47	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences; don't pad with intent, don't restate
48	  the plan.
49	- **Plan bullets** (the what/when): formality differs by surface:
50	  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per commit; see
51	    [Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
52	    per-step title + `(current)` / `(done)` form.
53	  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering; formalized only when the entry is
54	    picked up into a cycle.
55	
56	### Semicolons inside bullets
57	
58	A bullet that joins multiple clauses with semicolons (`A; B; C`) is a list hiding inside
59	running prose: break the clauses into sub-bullets so the structure shows. Semicolons in running
60	prose (intro paragraphs, sentence-joins) are fine. Not absolute: very short clauses or tight
61	pairs can stay joined inside a bullet when breaking would be more noise than signal.
62	
63	### Typeable punctuation only
64	
65	Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal. Banned: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`.
66	None can be entered without a compose key or a paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em
67	dash next to option syntax reads as another flag. Unlike the semicolon rule above this one is
68	absolute: they cost nothing to write and are paid on every read, so a soft rule accumulates
69	them.
70	
71	`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no single replacement, because an em
72	dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:
73	
74	- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading and a paragraph. Make the body
75	  sub-bullets.
76	- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) takes a colon, which keeps a
77	  glossary or a command list at one line per entry.
78	- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Often the aside should just
79	  go.
80	
81	Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive,
82	so `## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see
83	[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same
84	commit.
85	
86	Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker), plus commit titles and
87	everything under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is
88	the surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in
89	prose. It applies going forward; existing text converts when touched. A code span is not exempt
90	by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section names them.
91	A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
92	`` `.expect(...)` ``.
93	
94	Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
95	commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits
96	in a code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching
97	`git log --grep` and breaks the verbatim identity that
98	[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) requires between
99	a commit title, its chores header, and its `## Done` entry.
100	
101	### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)
102	
103	A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description share a *title* shape, a
104	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`,
105	an optional `(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail.
106	They differ in the title's prefix / marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies are
107	file-by-file, ladder / chores conceptual (see "Bullet *content* differs by surface" above). The
108	shared template:
109	
110	```
111	<optional - X.Y.Z[-N]> <title>   # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
112	<optional prose intro>
113	  - <optional item>
114	    <optional prose intro>
115	      - <optional sub-item>
116	      ...
117	```
118	
119	The three surfaces apply it as:
120	
121	- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the title is prefixed with the version
122	  (`X.Y.Z-N <title>`) and carries a `(current)` / `(done)` marker. The bare three-element
123	  `X.Y.Z` (no `-N`) is the close-out step. Detail is bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
124	- **Chores section** (`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`): no version prefix, since the `##` header
125	  *is* the bare title, with a `Commits: [[ref]]` line first under it (empty until backfilled;
126	  see [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
127	- **Commit description**: no version prefix, and the title is the <=72-col first line; the body
128	  is the prose (file-by-file for the work repo, per
129	  [Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow)).
130	
131	The title is **identical** across all three for a given step, so a step's ladder entry, its
132	chores `##` header, and its commit title line up verbatim; pick the commit title first and
133	reuse it.
134	
135	That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct
136	descriptive title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The cycle's chores
137	section header carries the anticipated *close-out* title. To keep a cycle's commits collectable
138	with one `git log --grep`, give the step titles a common greppable stem (e.g. `config loader`).
139	
140	## Speculation marker
141	
142	Durable text the bot writes (instruction files, `notes/`, commit bodies, chores sections)
143	should stick to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism,

# Prose and durable text

How long-lived text is written on this project: the prose shape, the punctuation rules, and the
commit-title identity. Read this before writing durable text (notes files, commit messages, doc
comments, chores sections).

Universal file, pinned to vc-x1-work-repo-template; do not edit here. Project overrides go in
[custom.md](../custom.md).

## Prose form

Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why*
or the high-level *what*, then a `-` bullet list for the details. Wrap lines at <=100 cols,
commit titles and bodies at <=72 (bullet continuations indent two spaces); existing text
re-wraps when touched, no mass sweeps. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they hide the structure
that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their relationship is
the same failure at sentence scale; see [Semicolons inside bullets](#semicolons-inside-bullets)
and [Typeable punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).

Surfaces that use this shape:

- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files; see
  [Doc comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The <=72-col title is the
  commit-specific add-on; see [Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`; see
  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- Todo and Done entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure
  one-liners are still fine.

Bullet *content* differs by surface:

- **Commit bodies**: bullets are file-by-file, one bullet per file changed, file plus a
  one-line gist (e.g. `README.md: new Overview intro`), detail as sub-bullets in short sentence
  fragments (full sentences are discouraged). Source of truth for the mechanical edit list.
- **Chores / todo / done**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what
  landed and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit
  list; see
  [Chores section content](notes.md#chores-section-content-no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).

### Problem + plan shape

`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores section intros, and `## Todo` entries use a sharper form
of the same shape:

- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences; don't pad with intent, don't restate
  the plan.
- **Plan bullets** (the what/when): formality differs by surface:
  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per commit; see
    [Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
    per-step title + `(current)` / `(done)` form.
  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering; formalized only when the entry is
    picked up into a cycle.

### Semicolons inside bullets

A bullet that joins multiple clauses with semicolons (`A; B; C`) is a list hiding inside
running prose: break the clauses into sub-bullets so the structure shows. Semicolons in running
prose (intro paragraphs, sentence-joins) are fine. Not absolute: very short clauses or tight
pairs can stay joined inside a bullet when breaking would be more noise than signal.

### Typeable punctuation only

Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal. Banned: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`.
None can be entered without a compose key or a paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em
dash next to option syntax reads as another flag. Unlike the semicolon rule above this one is
absolute: they cost nothing to write and are paid on every read, so a soft rule accumulates
them.

`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no single replacement, because an em
dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:

- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading and a paragraph. Make the body
  sub-bullets.
- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag) takes a colon, which keeps a
  glossary or a command list at one line per entry.
- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two sentences. Often the aside should just
  go.

Converting a heading moves its anchor. The em dash strips but the spaces on both sides survive,
so `## A — B` slugs to `#a--b` while its colon form slugs to `#a-b` (see
[Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Re-point inbound links in the same
commit.

Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker), plus commit titles and
everything under `src/`: doc comments, inline comments, and any user-visible string. Source is
the surface a human edits and greps most, so an untypeable character costs more there than in
prose. It applies going forward; existing text converts when touched. A code span is not exempt
by itself. Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this section names them.
A banned character doing a job is a use and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
`` `.expect(...)` ``.

Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an error message, an already-published
commit title) is transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, whether or not it sits
in a code span. It matters most for commit titles: converting one stops it matching
`git log --grep` and breaks the verbatim identity that
[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) requires between
a commit title, its chores header, and its `## Done` entry.

### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)

A ladder step, its chores section, and its commit description share a *title* shape, a
[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) title (`<type>: <desc>`,
an optional `(scope)` after the type: `feat(push): ...`) over [Prose form](#prose-form) detail.
They differ in the title's prefix / marker (below) and in bullet *content*: commit bodies are
file-by-file, ladder / chores conceptual (see "Bullet *content* differs by surface" above). The
shared template:

```
<optional - X.Y.Z[-N]> <title>   # <title> is the commit's `<type>: <desc>`
<optional prose intro>
  - <optional item>
    <optional prose intro>
      - <optional sub-item>
      ...
```

The three surfaces apply it as:

- **Ladder step** (`TODO.md` `## In Progress`): the title is prefixed with the version
  (`X.Y.Z-N <title>`) and carries a `(current)` / `(done)` marker. The bare three-element
  `X.Y.Z` (no `-N`) is the close-out step. Detail is bulleted, never `;`-joined inline.
- **Chores section** (`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`): no version prefix, since the `##` header
  *is* the bare title, with a `Commits: [[ref]]` line first under it (empty until backfilled;
  see [Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
- **Commit description**: no version prefix, and the title is the <=72-col first line; the body
  is the prose (file-by-file for the work repo, per
  [Per-commit flow](../notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow)).

The title is **identical** across all three for a given step, so a step's ladder entry, its
chores `##` header, and its commit title line up verbatim; pick the commit title first and
reuse it.

That identity is **per step**, not per cycle: each step in a cycle gets its own distinct
descriptive title, never one shared cycle title uniquified by a step marker. The cycle's chores
section header carries the anticipated *close-out* title. To keep a cycle's commits collectable
with one `git log --grep`, give the step titles a common greppable stem (e.g. `config loader`).

## Speculation marker

Durable text the bot writes (instruction files, `notes/`, commit bodies, chores sections)
should stick to observations and direct descriptions of the code or data. If a mechanism,
hypothesis, or causal claim enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
reader can tell the measured from the inferred.

**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader (or the bot on a later
session) can pick it up as a known fact when it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction
worth keeping visible in the written record.

**How to apply:** observations and factual descriptions need no marker. Prefix with
"We think ..." (or a close variant like "Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism
("X wins because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal state"), a
prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any reasoning not directly supported by the data
on hand.

## Plain synopsis after technical explanations

When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation (measurement theory, statistics,
hardware behavior), end it with a short plain-language synopsis, no jargon and no symbols, so
the reader can check their understanding against the technical version.

**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread; the plain form catches
misunderstandings early, when they are cheap.

**How to apply:** conversation only, not notes files (a notes entry should already lead with
the why). Mark it clearly (e.g. "The plain version:"). A reply that is already plain needs no
synopsis.

##### 0.78.0-5 refactor: jj-lib reads

The facade's internals flip: in-process through jj-lib is now
the default read path, and spawning is the carve-out rather
than the mechanism. The seam the DRY-facade cycle bought is
what made this a one-module change: every caller kept its
signature, so push, squash-push, sync, init and the registry
checks moved without being edited.

- The routing is per revset, not per call site, because the
  revs are runtime values: squash-push's source/target default
  to `@`/`@-` but are user-overridable, so no static split of
  the call sites exists. `references_working_copy` decides: a
  `@` is working-copy syntax (`@`, `@-`, `ws@`) unless it has
  symbol characters on both sides, the remote-bookmark form
  (`name@remote`).
- Working-copy revsets keep the spawn path on purpose (the
  ladder's standing caveat): the CLI auto-snapshots, so "is
  `@` empty right now?" answers about the filesystem, while an
  in-process `load_at_head` would answer about the last
  snapshot. Those reads move at `-6` with the mutation lift.
- The raw `log(repo, rev, template)` primitive is gone from
  the facade surface: jj-lib has no template engine (templates
  live in jj-cli), so its one caller, sync's bookmark-heads
  probe, became the typed `cids_short_of`.
- `rev_exists` and sync's `try_commit_id` now classify the
  unresolvable-revision error through one helper,
  `is_no_such_revision`: a typed
  `RevsetResolutionError::NoSuchRevision` downcast on the
  in-process path, the old stderr substrings on the spawn
  path. A first taste of the `-7` principle that
  classification is by variant, not wording.
- Parity is pinned by tests: the in-process accessors are
  compared against spawned `jj log` templates on a fixture
  repo, with revs pinned to concrete commit ids so the tests
  stay on the in-process path.
- `bookmark_list` / `bookmark_list_all` still spawn: their
  consumers parse the CLI listing textually. They are not
  `jj log` templates, so not this rung's scope; where they
  land (a typed view query, or a rider on `-6`) is an open
  ladder question.

message.content: I'm confused log is renamed log_spawn and several routines like chid_of use it but have grown more code, explain

content.text:
Before this rung, every helper was a one-liner because there was only one mechanism: build a `jj log -T <template>` argument list and spawn it. `chid_of` was literally just `log(repo, rev, "change_id.short(12)")`.

Now each helper contains **two implementations of the same query**, and picks one at runtime:

```rust
pub fn chid_of(repo: &Path, rev: &str) -> Result<String> {
    if references_working_copy(rev) {
        return log_spawn(repo, rev, "change_id.short(12)");   // path 1: the old code
    }
    Ok(commits_of(repo, rev)?                                  // path 2: new, in-process
        .iter()
        .map(common::format_chid)
        .collect())
}
```

- **Path 1 (spawn)** is the entire old implementation, unchanged, demoted to a private helper. The rename `log` -> `log_spawn` is just labeling: it's no longer "the way reads work", it's "the spawn fallback". It exists because revsets touching the working copy (`@`, `@-`, `@ & empty()`) need jj's auto-snapshot to answer correctly — e.g. push's "does `@` have uncommitted changes *right now*?" — and snapshotting in-process is an op-store write, which this cycle defers to the mutations rung `-6`.
- **Path 2 (in-process)** is where the growth comes from. A spawned `jj` did resolve-revset-and-format for us behind one string template; in-process, those steps become visible Rust: `commits_of` loads the repo and resolves the revset to `Commit` objects, then each helper does in code what its template string used to do — `format_chid` for `change_id.short(12)`, `c.id().hex()` for `commit_id`, `c.description()` for `description`, `commit.is_empty(...)` for `empty`.

So the extra lines aren't added behavior — they're the template language's work being spelled out, plus one `if` deciding which engine answers. At `-6`, when mutations (and snapshotting) move in-process, the `if references_working_copy` branches and `log_spawn` itself are deleted, and each helper shrinks back to just its path-2 body.

Why the branch lives *inside* the helpers rather than at the call sites: the revset is often a runtime value (squash-push's source/target default to `@`/`@-` but the user can override them with anything), so no call site knows statically which engine it needs.

The plain version: the old one-line functions were thin wrappers around one tool, the jj command line. Now each function knows two ways to answer, the new built-in way and the old spawn way, and a small check picks between them. The old code didn't shrink, it moved into `log_spawn`; the new code is the built-in way written out longhand. The check and the spawn path are temporary scaffolding that the mutations rung removes.

content.text:
It's a fair instinct — the scaffolding exists only because reads land before the thing that would make it unnecessary. But I'd keep the order and push -5 as built. The reasoning:

**Why reads-first was chosen (and still holds):**

- **-6 is the risky rung; -5 shrinks it.** The mutation lift is the workspace/transaction/op-store machinery — the part of this cycle that can actually corrupt state and the reason the version gate exists. Landing reads first means -6's diff is *only* the dangerous part, reviewed on its own, with the resolve/format machinery already proven in production for a rung's worth of real use. Merged, one push changes every read *and* every write in the same diff, and a regression found later bisects to "the giant commit".
- **Reverting stays cheap.** If in-process reads turn out to misbehave somewhere, -5 reverts without touching mutations. If -6 misbehaves, it reverts without taking the reads with it. A merged rung couples their fates.
- **The scaffolding is smaller than it looks, and half of it survives -6.** `log_spawn` dies at -6, but the `references_working_copy` classification probably doesn't: even fully in-process, "is `@` empty right now?" still needs a *snapshot first, then read* step that plain reads don't. The likely -6 shape is that the same check routes to "snapshot, then answer" instead of "spawn". So the part of -5 that took actual thought — knowing which revsets are working-copy-relative — is a keeper; only the one-line spawn fallback is throwaway.

**Why -6-first doesn't win:** it would avoid the two-path helpers, but the cost is inverted risk ordering — the op-store lift would land with zero of its read-side machinery pre-validated, and -5 afterwards would be a near-trivial rung. You'd be spending review attention on the safe part after the dangerous part already shipped.

**And practically:** -5 is built, validated, and its cost is already paid. Reordering now means discarding or reshaping done work to avoid scaffolding that -6 deletes in a few days anyway.

If we were standing at cycle open with nothing built, "merge them" would be a defensible call — the counterargument would be diff size and blast radius, and reasonable people could land either way. From where we are, separate-and-in-this-order is better on every axis except "temporary `if` branches exist for one rung".

The plain version: the extra code you noticed is temporary, but it's the cheap kind of temporary — a small detour that lets the scary step (-6) arrive alone, small, and easy to check. Combining the steps would save the detour but make the scary step bigger and harder to undo. I recommend pushing -5 as is and letting -6 delete the detour.

##### 0.78.0-6 refactor: jj-lib mutations

The workspace/transaction/op-store lift. A new `jj::engine`
module is the CLI's `WorkspaceCommandHelper` plumbing reduced
to what the facade's verbs need, written against jj 0.43's
`cli_util.rs` as the reference; the facade grows the five
publish-path verbs on top, and the `@`-read carve-out from
`-5` closes.

- The engine is three pieces: a settings loader replicating
  the CLI's config discovery (`/etc/jj`, `$JJ_CONFIG`, user
  files, `.jj/repo/config.toml`, `JJ_USER`/`JJ_EMAIL`), the
  snapshot cycle (git HEAD/refs import around the
  working-copy snapshot, under the CLI's own
  `git_import_export.lock`), and transaction finish (git HEAD
  reset + ref export, op commit, working-copy update).
  Colocation drives the git halves; these repos are
  colocated, so that fidelity is the bulk of the engine.
- Verbs: `commit`, `describe`, `bookmark_set`,
  `git_push_bookmark`, `git_fetch`. Call sites swapped in
  push, squash-push, sync, fix-desc, init, and repo_utils.
  The ladder's "bookmark track" had no call site to lift:
  jj-lib's `push_refs` marks pushed bookmarks tracked, which
  is the side effect init's no-`--allow-new` design relied on
  in the spawned form too.
- The `@`-read deferral resolves as predicted at `-5`:
  `references_working_copy` survives as the trigger, now
  routing to snapshot-then-read (`repo_for_read`) instead of
  to a spawn; `log_spawn` is deleted and
  `is_no_such_revision` drops its stderr-wording fallback,
  leaving only the typed `NoSuchRevision` downcast.
- Fetch returns typed changed-bookmark lines; sync's
  stderr-capture wrapper (`fetch_silent`) now just relabels
  them, keeping the clean-case silence it existed for.
- Documented deviations from the CLI, each at its function:
  no immutability preflights (rewrite targets are validated
  by callers), a small defaults layer for three keys whose
  defaults ship in the CLI's config files rather than
  jj-lib's, the auto-track map driven by
  `git.auto-local-bookmark` alone, and the fetch expression
  pinned to all-branches rather than the remote's refspec
  config.
- Still spawning after this rung: `jj squash` (squash-push),
  `jj new` / `jj rebase` / `jj op log` / `jj op restore`
  (sync, revert), `jj git clone` (clone), `jj diff --stat`
  (push preview), init's `gh` / `git init --bare` (the `-7`
  gix rider) / `jj git init --colocate` / `jj git remote
  add`, the facade's two bookmark listings, and the gate's
  `jj -V`, which is a spawn by definition. The migration
  stage's "removes spawning entirely" now reads as this
  cycle's five verbs plus a remainder with named homes.
- Validation is the existing integration suites now running
  entirely through the engine (init, push, squash-push, sync
  fixtures), plus facade tests pinning colocated-git export:
  after in-process commit / bookmark-set / describe, `git
  rev-parse` sees the same commit ids jj reports.

0.78.0-6 refactor: jj-lib mutations is built and validated. The summary:

**The engine** (`src/jj/engine.rs`, new, ~500 lines): jj-cli's `WorkspaceCommandHelper` plumbing reduced to what our verbs need, written against jj 0.43's `cli_util.rs` as reference:
- a settings loader replicating the CLI's config discovery (`/etc/jj`, `$JJ_CONFIG`, `~/.jjconfig.toml`, XDG config + `conf.d`, `.jj/repo/config.toml`, `JJ_USER`/`JJ_EMAIL`), so in-process commits carry your real identity;
- the snapshot cycle under the CLI's own `git_import_export.lock`: git HEAD import, working-copy snapshot, git refs import — the colocated fidelity is the bulk of the engine;
- transaction finish: git HEAD reset + ref export, op commit, working-copy update.

**The five verbs** on the facade: `commit`, `describe`, `bookmark_set`, `git_push_bookmark`, `git_fetch`; call sites swapped in push, squash-push, sync, fix-desc, init, repo_utils. "bookmark track" had no call site to lift — jj-lib's `push_refs` marks pushed bookmarks tracked, the side effect init already relied on.

**The `-5` carve-out closes**: `references_working_copy` survived as predicted, now routing to snapshot-then-read; `log_spawn` is deleted; `is_no_such_revision` is typed-only.

**Flagged for review** (each documented at its function): no immutability preflights on rewrites/pushes (callers validate); a small defaults layer for three keys whose defaults ship in the CLI's config files, not jj-lib's; auto-track driven by `git.auto-local-bookmark` alone; fetch pinned to all-branches. Still spawning: `jj squash`, `jj new`/`rebase`, `op log`/`op restore`, `git clone`, `diff --stat`, init plumbing (gh, `git init --bare` for `-7`), the two bookmark listings, and the gate's `jj -V`. No new `unwrap`/`expect` sites in non-test code.

**Validation**: fmt clean, clippy `-D warnings` clean, **528 tests pass** — the init/push/squash-push/sync integration suites now run entirely through the engine against real colocated fixtures, plus new facade tests pinning colocated-git export (`git rev-parse` agrees with jj after in-process commit/bookmark-set/describe). Installed at 0.78.0-6. `validate-todo` green.

One thing worth savoring: when you approve this push, `vc-x1 push` itself will run the new in-process commit, bookmark-set, and git-push for the first time on a live repo — the rung publishes itself through the code it adds.

Ready to commit.

Good eye — I looked at all five verbs with this question in mind. My take: no trait, probably no helper yet, and there's a cheap local cleanup if the repetition itself bothers you.

**What's actually repeated.** Three different things are entangled here:

1. **`tx.repo_mut()` appearing twice in a row.** This isn't logic duplication, just repeated accessor calls — each returns the same `&mut MutableRepo`. In our `commit` we could bind it once (`let mut_repo = tx.repo_mut();`) and use it for all three steps; the borrows are sequential so it compiles fine. Interesting aside: the jj CLI *can't* do this — its transaction wrapper invalidates an id-prefix cache on every `repo_mut()` call, so the repeated-call style in my code is an unexamined inheritance from the reference code, not a necessity. A one-line binding fixes the visual noise with zero abstraction.

2. **The `rewrite_commit(..).set_description(..).write()` chain** appears exactly twice (commit, describe). That's rule-of-three territory: a `redescribe(tx, &commit, desc)` helper would be fine, but the chain is jj-lib's own `CommitBuilder` idiom, and keeping it inline means anyone comparing our verbs against jj-cli's implementations sees the same shapes. I'd leave it.

3. **The frame** — `Engine::open`, `snapshot`, `start_tx`, ..., `finish_tx` — appears in all five verbs, and this is the real candidate. But the middles deviate in ways that make a closure wrapper (`with_mutation(repo, |eng, tx| ...)`) awkward today: `describe` early-returns *before* opening a transaction (no-op case), `git_push_bookmark` checks push stats between the git call and finish, and `git_fetch` both early-returns and carries a data result out. You'd need a signature with escape hatches for "don't finish" and "return a value", which is how a helper ends up harder to read than the five plain functions it replaced.

**Why I'd wait rather than skip forever:** `-7` is the index-lock retry, and the retry has to wrap exactly this frame — the lock acquisitions live in `start_working_copy_mutation` and the op-store write in `finish_tx`. When we build that, the retry's placement will force a decision about where the frame's one true home is, and the consolidation can earn itself there with a concrete requirement in hand instead of being speculative structure now.

A trait specifically I'd rule out: there's one engine type and no polymorphism dimension — nothing for a trait to abstract over.

So: if you'd like, I can fold the `let mut_repo = tx.repo_mut();` binding into `commit` now (it's the only verb with the double call), and we note the frame question as a `-7` design input rather than restructuring today.

The plain version: most of the lookalike lines are the library's own builder style, not copied logic. The one pattern that truly repeats across all five functions is the open-snapshot-transact-finish skeleton, but each function bends that skeleton differently, so a shared wrapper would need awkward special cases. The next rung has to wrap that same skeleton with retries anyway, so that's the right moment to unify it — with a function, not a trait.

message.content: I wonder if we should open eng and tx and share them?

content.text:
Yes to the direction — what you're describing is exactly the jj CLI's own architecture, and it's the natural end-state. But there are two different "shares" in the question, and they deserve different answers.

**Sharing `eng` (one Engine per repo per command run): yes, eventually.** The CLI builds one `WorkspaceCommandHelper` per invocation and everything the command does flows through it. Our current shape opens a fresh Engine — full workspace load, repo-at-head load, and a snapshot cycle — inside *every* facade call. A single `vc-x1 push` run does that maybe eight times across its stages (the `@`-emptiness checks, the two commits, two bookmark sets, the push). Each repeat after the first is a no-op snapshot, so it's wasted milliseconds rather than wrong behavior, but the coherence argument is real: a command would act on one continuously-maintained view (every `finish_tx` already updates `eng.repo`, so a shared engine stays current as mutations flow through it). The verbs would become methods on the engine, and push.rs would hold two engines (work and bot) across its stages.

**Sharing `tx` across verbs: no — that one changes semantics.** One transaction per verb means one operation in the op log per step, which is what the spawned form produced and what two design decisions lean on: push's "rerunning is safe, every stage no-ops" property, and sync's revert, which rewinds by op id and needs stage-granular ops to rewind to. Fusing a whole push into one tx would make crash recovery *cleaner* (nothing committed until the end) but it changes the op-log shape users and `vc-x1 revert` see. If we ever want that, it's its own decision with sync's revert redesigned alongside — not a byproduct of DRYing the code.

**When:** not in this rung. -6 is validated and reviewable as a faithful lift; reshaping the facade API now would fold an architecture change into an already-large diff. And it's bigger than the -7 retry fix should absorb — the ladder culture here is one thing per rung. My recommendation: insert a rung between them —

- `0.78.0-7 refactor: engine session` — verbs become methods on a shared per-repo Engine; push/sync/squash-push stages thread it through; one op per verb preserved
- `0.78.0-8 fix: jj-lib index-lock retry` — renumbered from -7, and it lands nicely *after* the session exists, because the retry wants to wrap exactly the session's lock-and-commit points

The alternative is doing both in one rung since the retry is small once the session exists, at the cost of a two-purpose rung.

That's a ladder change, so it's your call: insert the session rung (my recommendation), fold session+retry into one rung, or park the idea as a Todo and land the retry on today's shape.

The plain version: sharing the opened repo handle across a command's steps is the right long-term shape and matches how jj itself is built. Sharing one transaction across steps is a different, riskier idea that would change what undo and re-run see, so I'd keep transactions per-step. Neither belongs in the commit we have ready now; I suggest adding a dedicated ladder step for the shared handle right after this one.
